passage:
Looking back, the poem was the start of it. Preeti read it to me at the bus stop in March, her voice shaking a little. "Pranav, be honest," she said. The middle verse didn't make sense to me. I said, "It's really good, honestly." She smiled and folded it away.
After that I noticed how often I said things were fine. Fine after the football trials I didn't make. Fine when Dad asked about the new school. Each "fine" ended the awkward moment quickly, and I liked that.
In June Preeti told another girl in our class, not me, that the magazine had rejected her poem. It stung, but I understood. Why would anyone bring the hard stuff to someone who only ever says nice things?

qa.q: Where did Preeti read her poem aloud?
qa.a: Preeti read it at the bus stop in March, her voice shaking a little.

qa.q: Why does Pranav keep saying things are "fine"?
qa.a: Pranav wants to escape awkward moments; each "fine" ended the discomfort quickly, even though it hid what Pranav really felt.

qa.q: What could Pranav have said about the poem that was both kind and honest?
qa.a: Pranav could have praised a line that worked and gently said the middle verse was confusing, which might have helped Preeti before she sent it out.

qa.q: Why might Preeti have taken her rejection news to another girl instead?
qa.a: She may have felt Pranav only ever says nice things, so she needed someone who would respond honestly to hard news.

grounding: A teenager calls Preeti's poem good and keeps saying 'fine' to dodge awkward moments, and the habit quietly costs real closeness.

passage:
Warden's note, Girls' Hostel B, 14 November.
Rukmini (Class 11) has told me "All good, ma'am" four times this week, each time with a bright smile and her eyes on the floor. Tonight her roommate Kiran showed me a dance video she had made for annual day and asked Rukmini's opinion. Rukmini said, "Perfect, don't change anything."
Twenty minutes later I found Rukmini on the back stairs, upset. Kiran had been ignoring her for days, she said, and she didn't know how to bring it up without a fight.
I sat with her and asked what she might say if a fight wasn't the only option. She tried a sentence out loud: "I miss you, and I've been feeling left out." She plans to tell Kiran tomorrow. I will check in with both girls after dinner.

qa.q: How many times did Rukmini say "All good, ma'am" this week?
qa.a: Rukmini said "All good, ma'am" four times this week.

qa.q: What was Rukmini feeling on the back stairs?
qa.a: She felt upset and left out because Kiran had been ignoring her, and she was afraid that raising it would start a fight.

qa.q: How did the warden support Rukmini?
qa.a: The warden sat with her and helped her try out a true sentence, "I miss you, and I've been feeling left out", instead of pretending everything was perfect.

qa.q: How might Kiran take Rukmini's "Perfect, don't change anything"?
qa.a: Kiran might take it as real approval and never learn that Rukmini felt left out, so the distance between them could quietly grow.

grounding: A teenage girl says she is fine and praises her roommate's video to avoid an awkward scene, while the real hurt stays unspoken.

passage:
Literature club notes, Thursday. Written by the club teacher.
Nilesh read his poem about his late grandfather's bicycle to the group today. It was long, and the middle verses repeated themselves. When he finished, he looked straight at Akash, his closest friend. Akash said, "Loved it, bro, it's perfect," and then went back to his phone. I noticed his knee bouncing the whole time.
After the session, Nilesh asked Akash to stay and help him cut it down for the inter-school round. Akash said he had tuition and left fast.
I caught Akash at the gate and asked, without any pressure, what he really thought. He said, "The ending is really good. The middle drags. But he'd be upset." I suggested he tell Nilesh the ending made him feel something, then name one verse to cut. He nodded slowly. Tomorrow I'll check in with both of them.

qa.q: What was Nilesh's poem about?
qa.a: It was about his late grandfather's bicycle.

qa.q: What does Akash's bouncing knee suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: It suggests Akash felt tense and awkward, because he did not believe the poem was perfect but was afraid Nilesh would be upset by the truth.

qa.q: What small step did the teacher suggest to Akash?
qa.a: The teacher suggested telling Nilesh that the ending made him feel something and then naming one verse to cut, which keeps both kindness and honesty.

qa.q: What might Nilesh want from Akash before the inter-school round?
qa.a: Nilesh wants real help from his closest friend; "it's perfect" gives him nothing to work with, and Akash leaving quickly may feel like distance.

grounding: It shows a teenager saying he loved a friend's poem to dodge an awkward moment, and how that habit can quietly replace real closeness.

passage:
Tuesday, 10:40 pm.
Preeti asked me again at the bus stop, "Nazia, are you okay? You've been so quiet." And I said, "I'm fine, just sleepy." That's the third time this week.
I'm not fine. She picked Rhea's group for the science project without even asking me, and then posted pictures of all of them at the café. I know it's small. I know she didn't mean it. But if I say it, she'll say sorry in that careful voice and it'll be weird on the bus for days.
So I smile and say fine. And she believes me, and we talk about the maths test instead, and it's okay. Except it isn't really okay. We used to tell each other everything. Now I have a whole list of things I haven't told her, and it keeps getting longer.
Maybe tomorrow. Maybe.

qa.q: How many times did Nazia say "I'm fine" to Preeti that week?
qa.a: That's the third time this week.

qa.q: Why does Nazia keep saying she is fine?
qa.a: Nazia feels hurt about being left out, but Nazia is scared of an awkward, careful apology and days of weirdness on the bus.

qa.q: What small step could help Nazia and Preeti stay close?
qa.a: Nazia could tell Preeti calmly, just once, that she felt left out of the project, instead of letting the list of unsaid things grow.

qa.q: How might Preeti feel if she learned Nazia had been hurt for days?
qa.a: Preeti might feel sad and a little shut out, because she asked twice and wanted to know how her friend was really doing.

grounding: It illustrates a teenager saying they are fine to avoid an awkward scene, and the habit slowly replacing real closeness.

passage:
After school in Nabha, Trisha pulled a folded paper from her bag at the chai stall. "I wrote a poem for the district contest. Read it. Honestly."
Parveen read it. The rhymes were forced, and the last verse made no sense. "It's really good," she said. "I loved the ending."
Trisha's face lit up. "Really? I was so nervous."
"Really," Parveen said, and sipped her chai too fast.
It was the third time this month. She had said she was fine when Trisha asked why she'd been so quiet. She had said Trisha's new haircut was nice. Each time it was easier than the awkward conversation.
Walking home, Parveen realised she didn't actually know whether Trisha would still like her if she said what she really thought. And Trisha didn't really know her either. The contest was next week.

qa.q: What did Trisha ask Parveen to read?
qa.a: A poem she wrote for the district contest.

qa.q: Why did Parveen say she loved the ending?
qa.a: Parveen felt awkward and wanted to dodge an uncomfortable moment, so praise felt easier than honest feedback.

qa.q: What could Parveen still do before the contest?
qa.a: Tell Trisha kindly which lines work and suggest looking again at the last verse, so Trisha gets real help in time.

qa.q: What does Trisha lose from Parveen's easy praise?
qa.a: Trisha loses useful feedback before the contest and, slowly, a friend who tells her what she truly thinks.

grounding: Shows a teenager telling a friend her poem is good to avoid awkwardness, and noticing the habit is replacing real closeness.
